title: Italy and Byzantium
hookLine: Jews have lived in Rome since before the Temple fell

cards: In the Roman Forum stands a stone arch built for a general named Titus. Look up at the inside wall: carved soldiers carry a great lampstand on poles, the Temple menorah, out of a city they have just burned.
A victory picture, made by the winners. Some Roman Jews keep a custom of never walking under that arch. And here's the strange part.
Their community was in Rome before the arch went up, and it is still there now that the empire that built it is gone.
Today, the old Jewish communities of Italy and Byzantium: people who stayed, generation after generation, in the same streets.

teach.b: Start with the oldest written traces.
The first book of Maccabees tells how Judah Maccabee sent envoys to Rome to make a treaty of friendship, before the Temple fell, and tradition in Rome's Jewish community points back to ties like it.
Then the New Testament gives two snapshots. The book of Acts mentions a couple who had to leave the city, in the King James words, "because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome."

teach.h: CALLED THE CHIEF OF THE JEWS TOGETHER.
teach.b: And when Paul reaches Rome, Acts says he "called the chief of the Jews together." Even in stories about someone else, a Jewish community is already living there. Now turn east.
When the Roman Empire split, its eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, is what historians call Byzantium.
Greek-speaking Jews lived across its towns, in Greece, in the islands, and in southern Italy, which Byzantium ruled for a long stretch.
Their descendants are sometimes called Romaniote Jews, and they kept their own prayer customs and poems.

teach.h: A FAMILY SCROLL THAT HANDS THINGS ON.
teach.b: From southern Italy comes a Hebrew family chronicle, the Scroll of Ahimaaz: a writer traces his ancestors through generations of teachers, poets and community leaders, with miracle stories woven in.
Life under Byzantine rule was not easy; the same scroll remembers an emperor who pressed Jews to convert, and times of hardship. But the communities held.
And here's the thread for tomorrow: teachers and families from Italy carried learning north, over the Alps. An old community is a place that keeps handing things on.

how: Roman Jews and Romaniote Jews keep their own synagogue customs and prayer traditions, distinct from both Ashkenazi and Sephardi rites, and some still gather in historic synagogues in Rome and in Greece.

games.why: Acts mentions a couple who left because of Claudius, yet later Paul calls the chief of the Jews together in Rome. The community was there again.

practice: Bring to mind the oldest community near you: a synagogue, a church, a mosque, a temple, a neighborhood that has kept its name. Who first gathered there, and what did they carry with them, a language, a recipe, a song?
If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for the people who stayed.

wordCard.voice: Romaniote. The name for Greek-speaking Jewish communities of the old Byzantine Empire, who kept their own prayer customs and poems for generations. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: old communities. This one outlasted the empire that built the arch. That's day nine hundred seventeen.
